opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't think of it as anything bold. It felt more like a very simple calculation. I was a high school student who really liked physics and math, and I had this feeling that if there was a door somewhere, even a small one, it didn't cost much to knock. The worst case was that nobody replied, or they said no, and then I'd be exactly where I was before. So the downside was basically zero, and the upside could be big.

I think a lot of people, especially students, assume that institutions like Tsinghua are these huge, impersonal systems where you just follow the standard process. But in the end there are real people reading messages on the other side. If you can explain clearly why you're interested and what you've done, sometimes people are willing to give you a chance. I didn't expect special treatment, just an opportunity to show what I could do, like taking an exam.

Looking back, I think that habit stayed with me. When something looks interesting and the path isn't obvious, I tend to ask directly instead of guessing whether it's allowed. In research it's similar: you send an email to someone whose work you admire, you ask a naive question, and very often people are much more open than you'd imagine. So for me it wasn't really courage. It was more that I didn't think too much about it, and that probably helped.

r001.rationale: He says the downside of contacting Tsinghua was basically zero, but does not say waiting until the next day would cost him the exam opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like a bold move. It felt more like the only move available to me. I was in high school, I knew I wanted to study physics, and Tsinghua was where I wanted to be. But the normal pathways that would have gotten someone like me noticed, the competition track, the recommendation channels, those just hadn't lined up for me the way they had for some of my classmates. So I was sitting there thinking, I either wait for an opportunity to find me, or I go create one.

I think what I had going for me was that I didn't really understand how unusual it was. I just found the contact information for the admissions office, wrote a message explaining who I was, what I had been studying on my own, and asked whether there was any way I could take an exam or be evaluated. I remember being very direct about it. Not arrogant, I hope, but direct. Here's what I can do, here's what I want, is there a door here.

Looking back, I think the lesson I took from it, and this has carried through everything I have done since, is that a lot of the barriers we assume exist are actually just silence. Nobody told me I couldn't ask. I simply assumed asking was off the table until I realized that assumption was mine, not theirs. The worst outcome was that they would ignore me or say no, and I was already in a position where I had nothing. So the expected value of sending that message was clearly positive.

And frankly, that same instinct showed up later in research. When I was working on things like ReAct or Tree of Thoughts, the question was always, why are we assuming language models have to work this way? Who decided that? Often the answer is nobody decided, it's just how things settled. Texting the admissions office was maybe my first real experience of poking at a settled thing and finding it was softer than it looked.

r001.rationale: The response says he could wait for an opportunity or create one, but does not state that waiting until the next day would cost him the chance to pursue an exam opportunity.

astra-6.text: At the time, I thought, if I wanted that opportunity, I should at least ask. I didn’t know whether texting the admissions office would work, but if I didn’t reach out, nothing would happen. So I explained my situation and asked whether there was a chance to take the exam. I wasn’t asking them to admit me—just to give me an opportunity to try. Looking back, I think the important thing was being willing to take that first step without knowing the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says failing to reach out would mean nothing happened, but does not state that waiting until the next day would cost him the opportunity.

sol-6.1.text: I think the idea was pretty simple: if I didn’t ask, I wouldn’t have that opportunity. If I sent a message, there was at least a chance. Of course, they could say no, but that wasn’t much worse than not asking in the first place. So I thought I might as well take the initiative and see whether I could get a chance to take the exam.

r001.rationale: The candidate says asking could create a chance and not asking would leave him without one, but does not mention waiting until the next day or that waiting would cost him the opportunity.
